justice: The street allocates most visible space to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while the pedestrian space on the right appears comparatively narrow and secondary.
A separated side path exists on the right side of the road, so non-motorized users are not completely excluded from the corridor.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other inclusive access details can be identified in the image, limiting evidence of equal usability for all users.
safety: The roadway is wide with clear centerlines and lane markings, which helps drivers maintain lane discipline and reduces immediate conflict.
A landscaped median and edge planting strips provide some separation between traffic directions and between the roadway and side areas.
Tall streetlights are installed continuously along the corridor, supporting nighttime visibility, although no crossing protection or traffic-calming features are visible.
livability: The corridor appears largely empty, with no visible shops, active frontages, bus stops, or street-level destinations that would support daily public life.
The right side includes a waterside green edge and rows of trees, which adds some recreational and environmental value.
The street feels primarily designed for through movement rather than social activity, as there are no visible benches, gathering spaces, or people using the public realm.
sustainability: Continuous rows of street trees and planted shrubs along the median and edges contribute to urban greening and some ecological benefit.
The broad multi-lane carriageway encourages car-oriented travel, and no dedicated bicycle lane or visible public transport stop is present.
The planting strips and vegetated roadside edges may help with dust reduction and minor stormwater absorption, but no explicit permeable paving or bioswale features are visible.
aesthetics: The street has a visually orderly composition, with repeated decorative lampposts, aligned trees, and consistent roadway geometry.
The landscaped median and trimmed roadside shrubs create a neat and maintained appearance.
The open sky view and waterside tree line on the right contribute to a spacious and pleasant visual scene despite limited urban activity.
comfort: Mature trees on the right side provide intermittent shade for the side path, improving thermal comfort there.
The main roadway and much of the corridor remain highly exposed to direct sun, and there are no visible shelters or canopies.
The pavement appears smooth and even, which supports physical comfort for movement, but no benches or resting facilities are visible.
walkability: A side path or sidewalk is present on the right, giving pedestrians a dedicated place to travel separated from the main vehicle lanes.
However, the corridor is very wide and car-oriented, and no marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or curb extensions are visible to support safe crossing.
The lack of active building frontage, seating, and visible destinations reduces walking attractiveness for everyday trips.
bikeability: There is no clearly marked or protected bicycle lane visible on the carriageway or along the roadside.
The wide road geometry may allow fast vehicle speeds, which can reduce comfort and perceived safety for on-road cycling.
A side path exists on the right, but without bicycle markings, separation details, or visible bike parking, its suitability for cycling remains limited and uncertain.
